Your Mac is an **Apple M1** with **8 cores** (4 performance and 4 efficiency) and 16 GB RAM. For each phase I recommend:

| Phase | CPUs | Memory | What's running |
|---|:---:|:---:|---|
| **Now (Phases 1–3)** | **4** | **4 GB** | Postgres, later Redis |
| Phases 4–6 (load testing, Kafka) | 6 | 6–8 GB | Postgres, Redis, Kafka or Redpanda, Grafana, several services |
| Phase 8 (local Kubernetes) | 6 | 8 GB | A kind or k3d cluster plus everything above |

Also set **Swap to 1 GB** and leave the disk limit at its default.

**Why 4 CPUs and not all 8:**
- Docker Desktop runs a Linux **virtual machine**, and the CPU setting is a **cap** on that VM. It doesn't reserve the cores, so idle containers don't steal them.
- Your NestJS app (`npm run start:dev`), the TypeScript compiler, your editor and your browser all run **outside** Docker on macOS. They need cores too. Giving Docker everything makes your whole machine feel slow under load.
- Postgres on a single developer machine barely uses one core. You'll only need more once we add Kafka and load testing in Phase 4.

Set it in **Docker Desktop → Settings → Resources → CPU limit**, then click **Apply & restart**.

> 💡 **Platform-engineer habit:** in production, every container gets explicit **CPU and memory requests and limits**. They show up in Kubernetes manifests in Phase 8. What you're doing now is the laptop version of the same idea: give each workload a budget so one runaway process can't starve the rest.

## What a Compose file is

`docker-compose.yml` is a **declarative** description of the containers your app needs. It says *what* you want running, not *how* to start it step by step. Running `docker compose up` reads the file and makes reality match it.

For now we need **one service: Postgres.** Your NestJS app runs outside Docker, directly on your Mac (`npm run start:dev`), and connects to Postgres through `localhost:5432`.

## The building blocks

| Key | What it means | Our requirement |
|---|---|---|
| `services:` | The list of containers | One: `postgres` |
| `image:` | Which prebuilt image to run, from Docker Hub | `postgres:16-alpine` (a pinned major version on a small Alpine base) |
| `container_name:` | A friendly name for `docker ps` | Optional, e.g. `banking-postgres` |
| `restart:` | What happens if it crashes or Docker restarts | `unless-stopped` |
| `environment:` | Variables passed into the container. The official Postgres image reads `POSTGRES_USER`, `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` and `POSTGRES_DB` the **first time** it starts. | Values come **from your `.env`**, not typed in the file |
| `ports:` | `"HOST:CONTAINER"` mapping | Makes the container's 5432 reachable as your Mac's 5432 |
| `volumes:` | Where data is stored | A **named volume** mounted at Postgres's data folder |
| `healthcheck:` | A command Docker runs repeatedly to ask "are you actually ready?" | Uses `pg_isready` |
| top-level `volumes:` | Declares the named volume | Needed so Docker creates and keeps it |

## Your skeleton: fill in the `???`

```yaml
services:
  postgres:
    image: ???                    # the image + tag from the requirements
    container_name: banking-postgres
    restart: ???
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${???}       # read from .env
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${???}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${???}
    ports:
      - "???:???"                 # host:container
    volumes:
      - ???:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${???} -d ${???}"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

volumes:
  ???:                            # the same volume name you used above
```

**How the `${…}` values work:** Compose automatically reads a file named `.env` in the same folder and substitutes its variables. So create `.env` next to the compose file:

```env
POSTGRES_USER=banking
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pick-a-local-password
POSTGRES_DB=banking_dev
```

You'll add `DATABASE_URL` to that same `.env` in Step 4 (Prisma). Its format is `postgresql://USER:PASSWORD@localhost:5432/DB`. You'll work out the exact value from the three variables above.

## ⚠️ Fix your `.gitignore` before anything else
It currently contains **only** `node_modules`. Before your first commit, add at least:
- `.env`, so your secrets never go to GitHub
- `dist/`, which is build output
- `*.tsbuildinfo`, a compiler cache (you have one at the root right now)

- `.DS_Store`, macOS junk (you have one in the repo)

The error is actually a good sign. Docker read your file and tried to fill in the `${…}` placeholders. The file still contains the skeleton exactly as I wrote it, so the `???` blanks are there for **you** to replace. 😄 Docker can't find a variable named `???`, so it gives up.

It's also good to see `.env` and `.env.example` already created with the right three keys. 👍

## How to read the error
> `invalid interpolation format for services.postgres.environment.POSTGRES_USER … ${???}`

- **"interpolation"** means swapping `${NAME}` for the value of `NAME` from `.env`.
- **`services.postgres.environment.POSTGRES_USER`** is the **exact path** in the YAML where the problem is.
- **`${???}`** is what it found, and `???` isn't a valid variable name.

Reading error paths like this is something you'll do every day as a platform engineer.

## Hints for each blank

Replace every `???`. The answers are all in the requirements table from my last message, or in your own `.env`.

| Line | Hint |
|---|---|
| `image: ???` | The image name and tag from the requirements: Postgres version **16**, the small Alpine variant |
| `restart: ???` | The policy that restarts the container unless **you** stopped it |
| `${???}` under `environment` | Each one is the **name of a key in your `.env`**. Look at the left side of each line in `.env`. |
| `"???:???"` under `ports` | Postgres's default port, on the **host** side and the **container** side |
| `???:/var/lib/postgresql/data` | **Make up** a short volume name, e.g. something like `pgdata` |
| `pg_isready -U ${???} -d ${???}` | The same `.env` keys for the **user** and the **database name** |
| `volumes:` → `???:` at the bottom | The **same name** you made up for the volume above, so Docker knows to create it |

Delete the `# …` hint comments once you've filled each line, or leave them in. YAML ignores comments.

## Then run it again
```bash
docker compose up -d
```
```bash
docker compose ps
```

When STATUS shows **`(healthy)`**, you're done with this step. If you get a new error, paste it here and we'll read it together. Try to guess what it means before you paste it.

> 💡 About the `What's next: Debug this Compose error with Gordon` line: that's Docker's built-in AI assistant. It's fine to use, but try reading the error yourself first. That's the skill you're building.

content.text:
Your database is up: **`banking-postgres … (healthy)`**. 🎉 Your compose file is correct.

One small review note: you used `postgres:16` instead of `postgres:16-alpine`. Both work. Alpine is about 4× smaller (~100 MB vs ~400 MB), which means faster pulls in CI and a smaller attack surface. It's worth switching later. Not urgent.

I also checked that **only Docker is listening on port 5432**, so there's no hidden Homebrew Postgres that your app might connect to by mistake. 👍

## How a connection string is built

A database URL is just an address, built from the same values you already put in `.env`:

```
postgresql://USER:PASSWORD@HOST:PORT/DATABASE?OPTIONS
```

| Part | What it is | Where you find it |
|---|---|---|
| `postgresql://` | The protocol / driver | Always this for Postgres |
| `USER` | Database user | `POSTGRES_USER` in your `.env` |
| `PASSWORD` | That user's password | `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` in your `.env` |
| `HOST` | The machine running Postgres | Your app runs **on your Mac**, and Docker publishes the port there (`"5432:5432"`). So what's the host from your Mac's point of view? |
| `PORT` | The **host** side of your port mapping | The left number in `"5432:5432"` |
| `DATABASE` | Database name | `POSTGRES_DB` in your `.env` |
| `?schema=public` | Optional: which Postgres schema Prisma uses | Add it as written |

**Your task:** put the pieces together and add a fourth line to `.env`:

```env
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://...your assembled value...
```

Also add `DATABASE_URL` to `.env.example`, with a placeholder password, not your real one.

### Two gotchas
1. **Special characters in passwords.** If your password contains `@`, `:`, `/`, `#` or `?`, it breaks the URL, because those characters have meanings inside it. They have to be **URL-encoded** (`@` becomes `%40`). For a local password, the simplest fix is to use only letters and numbers.
2. **Newer Prisma versions may not read `.env` automatically.** Recent versions generate a `prisma.config.ts` file when you run `npx prisma init`. If Prisma later says `DATABASE_URL` is missing even though it's in `.env`, look for that file. We'll handle it together if it happens.

## Test it

After you've done Step 4 (`npm i -D prisma`, `npm i @prisma/client`, `npx prisma init`) and set the URL:

```bash
npx prisma db pull
```

At this point, an error saying the database is **empty** or has **no tables** means **success**: Prisma connected and found nothing yet. An error about authentication or connection means the URL is wrong. Read the error message and tell me which part of the URL you think is wrong.

---

## 🧠 Question about the URL

> **U1.** Your NestJS app uses `localhost` as the host because it runs on your Mac. In **Phase 2**, the app will run **inside its own container** in the same Compose file. Would `localhost` still work? If not, what would the host be, and why? (Hint: inside a container, `localhost` means *that container itself*.)

Your answer to U1 will show whether you understand Docker networking, which matters a lot in Phase 2.

Still open whenever you're ready: **K1–K4**, **D1–D2**, **A1–A3**.

content.text:
## Part 1: switching to `postgres:16-alpine`

### What's the difference?

Both images run **the same Postgres 16**. What differs is the Linux system underneath it:

| | `postgres:16` | `postgres:16-alpine` |
|---|---|---|
| Base OS | **Debian** | **Alpine** Linux |
| Size | ~430 MB | ~110 MB |
| C library | glibc, the standard one | musl, a minimal one |
| Tools inside | Many (bash, apt, …) | Very few (`sh`, `apk`) |
| Attack surface | Larger: more packages, more potential CVEs | Smaller |
| Pull speed in CI | Slower | Faster |
| Text sorting rules (collation) | glibc's locale data | musl's: **slightly different** |

**When teams pick Debian anyway:** when they need Postgres extensions or locale-specific sorting that behave better on glibc. For this project, Alpine is fine.

### ⚠️ The catch: don't reuse the old data

The two C libraries **sort text differently**. If you point an Alpine Postgres at a data folder **created by the Debian image**, text indexes built under Debian's sorting rules can quietly return wrong results under Alpine. This is a real production incident pattern called a collation mismatch.

Your database is **empty**, so the safe move is to wipe it and start fresh.

### Steps (you do these)

1. In `docker-compose.yml`, change the image line to `postgres:16-alpine`.
2. Stop the container **and delete the volume** (`-v`). Only do this because the database is empty:
   ```bash
   docker compose down -v
   ```
3. Start it again. Docker pulls the new image and creates a fresh volume:
   ```bash
   docker compose up -d
   ```
4. Check for `(healthy)`:
   ```bash
   docker compose ps
   ```
5. Optionally, confirm you're on Alpine:
   ```bash
   docker exec banking-postgres cat /etc/os-release
   ```

> 💡 **The real-world lesson:** changing a database image's base OS **in production** isn't a config tweak. It's a migration: back up, restore into the new image, rebuild the indexes. Today, an empty database made it free.

That partly answers **K1** too: `down` keeps the named volume and your data, while `down -v` deletes them.

---

## Part 2: U1 review 🟡

Your **reasoning** is right: today the container runs **only the database**, and your app runs directly on your Mac. **For now, `localhost` works.** ✅

But U1 asked about **Phase 2**, when the app moves into **its own container**. Then `localhost` **stops working**:

- Every container has its **own network**, as if it were a separate small computer.
- Inside the app container, `localhost` means **the app container itself**, and there's no Postgres in there.
- So the app would try to connect to itself and fail with *"connection refused."*

### What works instead
Compose puts all services in a file on a **shared private network** and gives each one a **DNS name equal to its service name**. Your service is called `postgres`, so inside the network the host is just `postgres`.

| Where the app runs | Host in `DATABASE_URL` | Port |
|---|---|---|
| On your Mac (today) | `localhost` | The **host** side of the mapping |
| In a container in the same Compose file (Phase 2) | `postgres` (the service name) | The **container** side: always 5432 |

This is exactly why the `docker-compose.yml` I showed you from Kwika-API earlier had `DATABASE_URL: postgresql://…@postgres:5432/…`. It overrides the host for the containerised app.

### Follow-up questions
> **U2.** Suppose you change the port mapping to `"5433:5432"` because something else on your Mac uses 5432. What port does **your Mac's app** use now? What port does a **containerised app** use? Why are they different?
>
> **U3.** Write the full `DATABASE_URL` the **Phase 2** containerised app would use, with a placeholder password.

Once Alpine is running and healthy, carry on with **Step 4 (Prisma)** and the `npx prisma db pull` test from my last message.

content.text:
Two things here: a quick U2 review, then the Prisma problem, which turns out to be an important lesson.

## U2: ✅ correct
The Mac's app uses **5433**, and a containerised app uses **5432**. The left side of `"5433:5432"` is a door **on your Mac**. Containers on the Compose network skip that door and talk to Postgres directly on its own port.

You skipped **U3** (the full Phase 2 `DATABASE_URL`). Try it. With U2 answered, it's one line.

Alpine healthy: confirmed ✅ (`postgres:16-alpine Up (healthy)`).

---

## The Prisma error: you installed a release candidate

I looked at `package.json` and the npm registry:

| Package | Installed | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `prisma` (CLI) | **`8.0.0-rc.23`** | A **release candidate**, published **today** |
| `@prisma/client` | `7.10.1` | Stable |

When you ran `npm i -D prisma`, npm installed whatever carries the **`latest`** tag. Prisma has (unusually) put the `latest` tag on a **version 8 release candidate**, while `@prisma/client`'s `latest` is still 7.10.1. So you got:

1. **A major-version mismatch between the CLI and the client.** They must always match, because the CLI generates the code the client runs.
2. **A pre-release CLI with different commands.** Version 8 doesn't recognise `db pull`, which is why you saw `No command registered for 'pull'`.
3. **A side effect:** `prisma@8` added a `postinstall` script (`prisma skills sync`). It **wrote AI-agent instruction files** into your repo under `.agents/`, `.claude/`, `.cursor/` and `.devin/`, and rewrote `prisma.config.ts` to configure them. You didn't ask for any of that. Those files now feed instructions to any AI tool that opens the repo, including me. I'm treating them as data, not instructions.

### 🎓 The platform lesson: version discipline
- **Never put pre-release versions (`-rc`, `-beta`, `-dev`) in money code.**
- **Pin matching versions** of packages that belong together, like the CLI and the client.
- **Be careful with packages published hours ago.** Many companies enforce a **minimum release age** (for example 7 days) before a new version can be installed. This protects against broken releases and against supply-chain attacks, where a hijacked package publishes a malicious version. Both Prisma versions here were published today.
- **Read your `postinstall` scripts.** They run code on your machine at install time.

## Fix it (you do this)

1. **Remove** the `"postinstall": "prisma skills sync || exit 0"` line from `package.json`.
2. **Pin both packages to the same stable version:**
   ```bash
   npm i -D prisma@7.10.1 --save-exact
   ```
   ```bash
   npm i @prisma/client@7.10.1 --save-exact
   ```
   `--save-exact` writes `7.10.1` instead of `^7.10.1`, so nothing upgrades silently.
3. **Delete the generated files:** the folders `.agents/`, `.claude/`, `.cursor/`, `.devin/` and the file `prisma.config.ts`. Look inside them first if you're curious. They're all `SKILL.md` files.
4. **Check** the CLI and client versions match:
   ```bash
   npx prisma -v
   ```
5. **Initialise again:**
   ```bash
   npx prisma init
   ```
   This should create `prisma/schema.prisma` and a new `prisma.config.ts`. Prisma 7 reads `DATABASE_URL` through that config file. If it doesn't load your `.env`, look for a `dotenv` import at the top of the new `prisma.config.ts`. You may need to `npm i dotenv`. Read the file before deciding.
6. **Run the test again:**
   ```bash
   npx prisma db pull
   ```
   Expected: an error saying the database is empty or has no tables. That means **success**.

### A related note on versions
You're on **Node v26**, which is very new. For a project you'll deploy, prefer the current **LTS** line (Node 24) and record it in `package.json` under `engines`. That way CI and production use the same version as your laptop. We'll do this properly in Phase 2, but keep it in mind.

---

## 🧠 Question
> **V1.** In `package.json`, what's the difference between `"^7.10.1"`, `"~7.10.1"` and `"7.10.1"`? And if versions are pinned in `package.json`, what does **`package-lock.json`** add? Should it be committed?

Paste the output of `npx prisma -v` and `npx prisma db pull` when you're done.

Good progress: the `postinstall` line is gone ✅ and both packages are pinned to exactly `7.10.1` ✅. There are three things in your output to deal with.

## 1. The error: step 3 isn't done yet
> `definePrismaConfig is not a function`

The `prisma.config.ts` that **Prisma 8** wrote is still there. It calls `definePrismaConfig`, which doesn't exist in Prisma 7, so the CLI crashes while loading its config before it can do anything, even `-v`.

The `.agents/`, `.claude/`, `.cursor/` and `.devin/` folders are also still there. Delete all five (the four folders and `prisma.config.ts`), then run `npx prisma -v` again.

> 💡 **Debugging habit:** when a tool fails *before* doing its job, suspect its **config file** first. The message even names it: *"Failed to load config file."*

## 2. `install scripts blocked`: this is your npm protecting you
You're on **npm 12**, which **blocks package install scripts by default** unless you approve them. That's exactly the supply-chain protection from my last message, built into npm. 🙂 It's a good default. You just need to approve the scripts you trust:

| Package | What its script does | Approve? |
|---|---|---|
| `@prisma/engines` | Downloads Prisma's **schema engine** binary, which `db pull` and `migrate` need | ✅ Yes, Prisma won't work without it |
| `prisma` | Pre-install environment checks | ✅ Yes |
| `fsevents` | Native macOS file-watcher used by dev tools | ✅ Optional but harmless, and makes `start:dev` watching faster |

**Steps:**
1. Look at what's blocked first:
   ```bash
   npm install-scripts ls
   ```
2. Approve the ones you trust:
   ```bash
   npm install-scripts approve @prisma/engines prisma fsevents
   ```
3. Run the install again so the approved scripts actually execute:
   ```bash
   npm install
   ```

Approvals should be saved to your project config. Check `git diff` afterwards to see where npm recorded them. That file gets committed, so your teammates and CI get the same approved list.

## 3. "5 vulnerabilities": don't run `npm audit fix --force`
I checked, and the results are **reassuring**:
- `npm audit --omit=dev` (production dependencies only) → **0 vulnerabilities** ✅
- All 5 come from **`@nestjs/mau`**, a **development-only** Nest CLI tool, through `inquirer`, `tmp` and `undici`.

They never ship with your API, so the risk is limited to your laptop. Note them and move on. `--force` can install **breaking major versions** to fix a dev tool, which isn't worth it.

> 🎓 **Platform habit:** separate the questions. "Does it affect production?" (`--omit=dev`) and "Does it affect developers or CI?" (all dependencies) are different risks with different urgency. In Phase 2, your CI pipeline will **fail the build** on high-severity vulnerabilities in production dependencies.

---

## Then continue
```bash
npx prisma -v
```
The CLI and `@prisma/client` should both show **7.10.1**. Then:
```bash
npx prisma init
```
```bash
npx prisma db pull
```

**Open questions still waiting:** V1 (`^` vs `~` vs exact, and the lockfile) and U3 (the Phase 2 `DATABASE_URL`). Paste your outputs and answers together.

content.text:
Nice debugging data. Your error output contains everything we need, so let's read it together.

```
Datasource "db": PostgreSQL database "$%7BPOSTGRES_DB%7D", schema "public" at "postgres:5432"
```

There are **two bugs** in that one line.

### Bug 1: `${…}` isn't expanded in `.env`
The database name came out as `$%7BPOSTGRES_DB%7D`. That's the literal text `${POSTGRES_DB}`, URL-encoded (`{` = `%7B`, `}` = `%7D`).

The reason: **Docker Compose** substitutes `${VAR}` in `docker-compose.yml`, but **`dotenv`**, the library Prisma uses to read `.env`, **doesn't** do substitution by default. Same syntax, different tool, different rules.

### Bug 2: host `postgres` — your U3 answer is right, just in the wrong place 😄
`postgresql://…@postgres:5432/…` is **exactly the correct Phase 2 URL** for an app running *inside* the Compose network. ✅ **Credit for U3.**

But today Prisma runs **on your Mac**, and your Mac has no DNS name called `postgres`, hence `Can't reach database server at postgres:5432`. From the Mac, the host is `localhost`.

### Fix (you do this)
In `.env`, write the URL with **literal values**: your real user, password and database name, `localhost`, port `5432`, and `?schema=public` at the end. Yes, this repeats the values from the lines above. That's normal for `.env` files. (`dotenv-expand` can do substitution, but it isn't worth the extra dependency.)

Then:
```bash
npx prisma db pull
```
Expected: an error saying the **database is empty**. That's success.

---

## Two more things I noticed

### `dotenv` is a phantom dependency ⚠️
`prisma7.config.ts` does `import "dotenv/config"`, but **`dotenv` isn't in your `package.json`**. It only works because another package happens to install it as a sub-dependency. If that package ever drops it, your config breaks for no visible reason. Code you import should always be declared:
```bash
npm i -D dotenv --save-exact
```

### Prisma 7's `init` installed AI skills too
It created `.claude/skills/`, `.windsurf/skills/`, `.agents/skills/` and `skills-lock.json` again. This time it's the stable version doing it. They're instruction files for AI coding tools, and they're now showing up in my context. I'm **not** following them, because they came from a package rather than from you.

My recommendation for a clean learning repo: **delete them** (the three folders plus `skills-lock.json`). If you'd rather keep them, at least add them to `.gitignore`. Your call either way.

Also: your `.gitignore` is fixed now, with `.env`, `dist/`, `*.tsbuildinfo`, `coverage/`, `.DS_Store` and Prisma's `/generated/prisma`. ✅ Nice.

---

## 🧠 Quick check
> **E1.** Here are three configs that all use `${…}` or a variable-like syntax: `docker-compose.yml`, `.env` read by `dotenv`, and a GitHub Actions workflow. Why is it dangerous to *assume* they all behave the same? What does this incident teach you about checking **which tool** is reading a file?

Still open: **V1** (`^`, `~`, exact versions and the lockfile). Send E1 and V1 with your `db pull` output.

Close, but the pieces went into the wrong **slots**. Here's what's in your `.env` now (password hidden), lined up against the pattern:

```
pattern:  postgresql:// USER      : PASSWORD @ HOST     : PORT / DATABASE    ?schema=public
yours:    postgresql:// localhost : ******** @ postgres : 5432 /             ?schema=public
```

| Slot | Should be | You have | |
|---|---|---|:---:|
| USER | `banking` | `localhost` | ❌ |
| PASSWORD | your password | your password | ✅ |
| HOST | `localhost` | `postgres` | ❌ |
| PORT | `5432` | `5432` | ✅ |
| DATABASE | `banking_dev` | *(empty)* | ❌ |

`localhost` went into the **user** slot instead of the **host** slot. The host still says `postgres`, and the database name is missing. Prisma then used `postgres` as the default database name, which is why the output said `database "postgres"`.

### The rule for reading a URL
- Everything **before `@`** is **who you are** (user:password).
- Everything **after `@`** is **where you're going** (host:port/database).

### The corrected line
Replace your `DATABASE_URL` line with this, putting your real password in place of `YOUR_PASSWORD`:

```env
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://banking:YOUR_PASSWORD@localhost:5432/banking_dev?schema=public
```

Then run:
```bash
npx prisma db pull
```

If it now says something like **"The introspected database was empty"**, that's success. 🎉 Prisma reached your Docker Postgres and found no tables yet, which is correct because we haven't designed any.

> 💡 **Reading the output was the right move.** `Datasource … database "postgres" … at "postgres:5432"` told you exactly what Prisma *thought* the URL meant. When a connection fails, compare that echo line to what you *intended*. It's the fastest way to spot a slot mix-up.

Once it works, update `.env.example` to the same shape with a placeholder password.

🎉 **"The introspected database was empty"** means it worked. Your stack is connected end to end:

```
Prisma CLI (your Mac) → localhost:5432 → Docker port mapping → postgres:16-alpine (healthy)
```

You hit and fixed five real-world problems to get here: the Docker daemon, a pre-release package, blocked install scripts, a config file that wouldn't load, and connection-string slots. That's what platform work actually looks like. 👏

I've updated the [README](README.md): Phase 0 is ✅, Phase 1 is 🟡, and there's a **Local setup** section showing how a new developer gets running.

---

## V1: 🟡 half right
`^` is right in spirit, but not "and everything above it." `~` is **not** exact.

| Spec | Allows | `7.10.1` can become… | Blocks |
|---|---|---|---|
| `^7.10.1` | Minor + patch | `7.10.2`, `7.11.0`, `7.99.0` | `8.0.0` (major) |
| `~7.10.1` | Patch only | `7.10.2`, `7.10.9` | `7.11.0` |
| `7.10.1` | Exact | nothing else | everything |

The idea behind it: **semantic versioning** is `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. A major bump means *breaking changes*. A minor bump means new features. A patch means bug fixes. `^` trusts publishers not to break anything below a major version, and `~` trusts them only with patches.

⚠️ **Watch out for versions starting with 0.** `^0.3.0` only allows `0.3.x`. Below 1.0, the minor number counts as "major." You have `@nestjs/observe: ^0.3.0` in your `package.json`.

**What the lockfile adds:** `package.json` only covers your **direct** dependencies, about 30 of them. But you have **465 packages** installed. `package-lock.json` records the **exact version and integrity hash of every one of them**, so every machine installs an identical dependency tree.
- ✅ **Always commit it.**
- In CI, use **`npm ci`**, not `npm install`. It installs exactly what the lockfile says and **fails** if `package.json` and the lockfile disagree.

## E1: you said "I can't say," which is fine. You lived the answer an hour ago:

| File | Read by | What `${VAR}` does |
|---|---|---|
| `docker-compose.yml` | Docker Compose | ✅ **Substituted** from `.env` and your shell, when the file is parsed |
| `.env` | `dotenv` (for Prisma or your app) | ❌ **Left as literal text**, which is exactly your `$%7BPOSTGRES_DB%7D` bug |
| GitHub Actions workflow | GitHub's runner | Uses its **own** `${{ … }}` syntax. Plain `${VAR}` inside a `run:` step is handled later by the **shell**. It never reads `.env` at all. |

**Lesson:** the **file extension doesn't decide the rules. The tool reading the file does.** Before you trust a syntax, ask *"which program parses this, and what are its rules?"* It's one of the most common causes of "works on my machine" bugs in CI/CD.

---

# Next: your first commit 📦

`git status` shows everything is still **untracked**. Nothing is committed yet. Good news: `.env` and `dist/` **don't** appear, so your `.gitignore` works. ✅

**Steps:**
1. **Decide about the AI skills** Prisma generated (`.agents/`, `.claude/`, `.windsurf/`, `skills-lock.json`). Delete them, or add them to `.gitignore`. Don't commit them by accident.
2. **Check `.env.example`.** It should have all four keys, including `DATABASE_URL` with a **placeholder** password.
3. **Review before staging:**

   git status

   Read every line. Is there anything you wouldn't want on a public GitHub repo?
4. **Stage and commit:**
   ```bash
   git add .
   ```
   ```bash
   git commit -m "chore: scaffold NestJS, Prisma 7 and Postgres 16 via Docker Compose"
   ```

> 💡 The `chore:` prefix comes from **Conventional Commits** (`feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:`, `docs:`, `test:`). Tools can generate changelogs and version numbers from it automatically. You'll use it from now on.

> **A1.** List the NestJS modules for Phase 1. Look at section 6 of [DESIGN.md](docs/DESIGN.md) for the scope. What does each module **own** (data and responsibility)?

content.text:
First commit `f768c95` reviewed ✅. `.env` was **not** committed, and the AI-skill folders stayed out of git. 👍 Two small follow-ups for your next commit:
- `skills-lock.json` *was* committed. Delete it, or add it to `.gitignore`, to match the folders.
- `.env.example` has only 3 keys. Add `DATABASE_URL=` so a new developer knows it's needed.

---

## A1: 🟡 you gave me *areas*, not *modules*
You pasted the scope table. That's the right raw material, but a **module** is a unit of code with **one clear owner of its data**. Two of your rows don't work as modules:

- **"Quality"** isn't a module. Validation, error handling and tests apply **everywhere**. These are *cross-cutting* concerns. In NestJS they live in **pipes** (validation), **exception filters** (errors) and **interceptors** (things like idempotency), shared through a `common/` folder.
- **"Ledger & transfers"** is really **two** modules with very different jobs:
  - **Ledger** is *how money is recorded*: postings, debits = credits, locks, balances.
  - **Transfers** is *a business use case*: check limits, check ownership, then ask the ledger to post.

  Later you'll add deposits, withdrawals, fees, interest and reversals, and **they'll all post to the same ledger**. If ledger logic sits inside "transfers," every new feature copies it.

## A2: 🟡 good security instinct, but a different question
"Forbidden from updating another user's data" is **authorisation**: customer X can't move money out of customer Y's account. That's a real rule, so keep it! It becomes an **ownership check** in Transfers.

A2 was asking about **module boundaries**, though. The industry rule is:

> **Each table has exactly one owner module. Only the owner writes to it.**

So **Transfers must never run `prisma.account.update({ balance })` or insert ledger lines itself.** It calls something like `ledgerService.post(...)`. Why?
1. **One place enforces the rules.** Debits = credits, row locks and lock ordering live in the Ledger *only*. If three modules write balances, three modules can get it wrong.
2. **It enables Phase 7.** If Transfers reaches into ledger tables, you can never split them into separate services.

I've added a **Module Boundaries** section (section 7) to [DESIGN.md](docs/DESIGN.md). It has the rules, a proposed module table with table ownership, and a dependency diagram. It's marked 🟡 because **you** need to settle three design decisions first:

---

## 🧠 Design decisions: think before answering

> **M1. Who owns the balance?** The `accounts` table looks like the natural place for the `balance` column. But the rule says only the Ledger writes money. Should the balance live on `accounts` (owned by Accounts) or in a ledger-owned table? What breaks with each choice?
>
> **M2. One transaction across modules.** A transfer must save the **idempotency record**, the **transfer row** and the **ledger postings** in **one database transaction**, because all of them have to commit or none of them. But each of those tables has a different owner. How can several modules take part in **one** transaction without breaking the "only the owner writes" rule? (Hint: think about what you could **pass** from one service to another.)
>
> **M3. The dependency direction.** In the diagram, `LedgerModule` depends on **no** other domain module. Suppose someone wants the Ledger to call `KycModule` to check tier limits before posting. Why is that a bad idea? Where should the limit check live instead?

These are the questions senior engineers argue about in design reviews, so take your time. Once they're decided, we'll generate the modules with the Nest CLI (you'll run the commands) and design the Prisma schema together.

content.text:
## Review: 1 of 3 correct

### ✅ M1: a ledger-owned table, correct
The balance lives in `ledger_balances`, owned by the Ledger. `accounts` only knows the number, status and owner. This puts the **one writer of money** rule straight into the schema. I've marked it ✅ in [DESIGN.md](docs/DESIGN.md).

### ❌ M2: Kafka can't give you one transaction
Kafka is the most interesting wrong answer, because it's the trap that real teams fall into.

**Kafka doesn't have database transactions.** When Transfers publishes an event, the Ledger writes its part *later*, separately. That means:
- For some time, the **transfer row exists but the money hasn't moved.**
- If the Ledger consumer crashes or rejects the event (say, insufficient funds), Transfers has **already committed**. Now you need compensation logic to undo it.
- You've swapped a guarantee (*all or nothing*) for **eventual consistency**: *it'll probably be correct… eventually.*

That trade-off is sometimes worth making **between microservices** in Phase 7, with sagas. **Inside one service, on one database, it's pure cost.** Remember: Kafka isn't in Phase 1 at all, and you got that right in Q5!

✅ **Answer: pass the transaction client.** Transfers opens one Prisma transaction and passes its `tx` handle into `ledgerService.post(tx, …)` and `idempotency.save(tx, …)`. Each service still writes **only its own tables**, but they all write **inside the same transaction**. One commit, one rollback.

> 🎓 Rule of thumb: **use database transactions where you can, and distributed patterns (events, sagas) only where you must.**

### ❌ M3: limit checks inside the Ledger cause trouble
It *sounds* safe ("the Ledger checks everything before posting!"), but consider everything that **also** posts to the Ledger:

| Posting | Should a KYC daily limit block it? |
|---|---|
| A customer's outgoing transfer | ✅ Yes |
| A **refund / reversal** of a failed transfer | ❌ **No.** Blocking a refund because a limit was "used up" is a customer-harming bug |
| A bank fee or interest credit | ❌ No |
| An admin correction | ❌ No |
| An **incoming** transfer to the customer | ❌ Usually no (different rule) |

If the limit check sits **inside** the Ledger, it either blocks all of these or fills up with `if (type !== 'refund' && …)` exceptions. It also makes the Ledger depend on KYC, so the most critical module now breaks whenever KYC changes.

✅ **Answer: in Transfers.** The **use case** knows the business context ("this is a customer-initiated transfer, so apply limits"). The **Ledger** is a dumb, strict accountant. It enforces **accounting rules only**: debits = credits, no overdraft, locks.

> 🎓 **Policy belongs at the top (use cases). Invariants belong at the bottom (ledger).** That split shows up in every well-designed system.

---

## 🧠 Re-test: same ideas, new situation
No options this time. Use what you just learned.

> **R1.** We add a **"Reverse transfer"** feature for admins. Which module owns the use case? List the steps it performs, and say which module does each step.

> **R2.** The KYC limit check passes, but the Ledger then rejects the posting with **insufficient funds**. The idempotency record was saved in the **same `tx`**. What happens to that idempotency record, and why is that what you want?

Answer these two and I'll mark M2 and M3 ✅. Then we generate the modules.

Let's go. R1 and R2 can wait. We'll come back to them when we build Transfers, which is where they apply naturally.

# Phase 1, Step 2: generating the module skeleton

## 1. Decide on the folder layout first

The Nest CLI puts everything directly in `src/` unless you tell it otherwise. With 8+ modules, that gets messy fast. A common industry layout:

```
src/
├── modules/          ← domain modules (one folder each)
│   ├── auth/
│   ├── customers/
│   ├── kyc/
│   ├── accounts/
│   ├── ledger/
│   ├── transfers/
│   └── notifications/
├── infrastructure/   ← technical plumbing
│   └── prisma/
├── common/           ← cross-cutting: filters, pipes, interceptors (later)
├── app.module.ts
└── main.ts
```

> 💡 Why `infrastructure/prisma` and not just `prisma/`? You already have a **root** `prisma/` folder with `schema.prisma`. Two folders with the same name in different places confuses people.

## 2. How the generator works

The pattern is `nest g <type> <name> <path>`. For example, the Ledger **module** and **service**:

```bash
npx nest g module ledger modules
```
```bash
npx nest g service ledger modules
```

That creates `src/modules/ledger/ledger.module.ts`, `ledger.service.ts` and `ledger.service.spec.ts`. It also **wires the service into the module** and **imports the module into `AppModule`** for you.

For a module that serves HTTP endpoints, add a **controller** too:

```bash
npx nest g controller accounts modules
```

## 3. What to generate (you work out the commands)

| Name | Path | Module | Service | Controller |
|---|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `auth` | `modules` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `customers` | `modules` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `kyc` | `modules` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `accounts` | `modules` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `ledger` | `modules` | ✅ | ✅ | ❓ **you decide** (see G1) |
| `transfers` | `modules` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `notifications` | `modules` | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| `prisma` | `infrastructure` | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |

⚠️ **Don't use `nest g resource`.** It generates CRUD endpoints, DTOs and "update/delete" boilerplate. **A ledger must never have update or delete endpoints.** We design each endpoint deliberately.

## 4. Check your work
1. Open `src/app.module.ts` and look at the `imports` array. What did the CLI add?
2. Build it:
   ```bash
   npm run build
   ```
3. Start it:
   ```bash
   npm run start:dev
   ```
   In the startup logs, look for lines like `[InstanceLoader] LedgerModule dependencies initialized`. There should be one for each module.
4. Run the generated tests:
   ```bash
   npm test
   ```
5. Commit with a message like:
   ```
   feat: add Phase 1 module skeleton
   ```

---

## 🧠 Questions while you generate

> **G1. Does the Ledger get a controller?** Customers will want to see their **transaction history** and **balance**. Should `GET /accounts/:id/transactions` live in a `LedgerController`, in `AccountsController`, or somewhere else? Remember the rule *only the owner writes*, and ask whether it also applies to **reading**.
>
> **G2. What `exports` does.** After generating, `ledger.module.ts` has `providers: [LedgerService]` but **no `exports`**. If `TransfersService` tries to inject `LedgerService` right now, NestJS will throw an error at startup. Why? What one line fixes it? And should `LedgerModule` **also** export anything that lets other modules write to ledger tables directly?

Paste the `imports` array from `app.module.ts` and your startup logs when you're done. If you get stuck on a command or an error, paste that too.

content.text:
Yes, generate all of them. Use **separate `module`, `service` and `controller` commands** for each row, not `resource`. Each ✅ in the table is one command.

## Why separate commands and not `resource`?

They're two different generators that produce **very different amounts of code**:

| | `nest g module` + `service` + `controller` | `nest g resource` |
|---|---|---|
| What it creates | **Empty** module, service and controller shells | A module, service and controller **plus ready-made CRUD**, with DTOs and entity files |
| Endpoints | **None.** You design each one. | **Five automatically:** `POST`, `GET` (all), `GET /:id`, **`PATCH /:id`**, **`DELETE /:id`** |
| Fits a bank? | ✅ Yes | ❌ No |

The problem is **`PATCH` and `DELETE`**. In a banking system:
- You **never update or delete a ledger entry**. You post a reversal instead (section 3 of your design doc).
- You **never delete a transfer**. It's a permanent financial record.
- You usually **don't delete accounts or customers** either. You *close* or *deactivate* them, because regulators require the history to be kept.

`resource` would hand you dangerous endpoints you'd then have to remember to delete. Empty shells force you to **add only what's allowed**.

> 🎓 **Principle:** in money systems, **start from nothing and add on purpose.** Don't start from everything and try to remove things.

## The pattern, using `auth` as the example

One command per ✅ in the `auth` row:

```bash
npx nest g module auth modules
```
```bash
npx nest g service auth modules
```
```bash
npx nest g controller auth modules
```

Then repeat for the other rows, changing the **name**, the **path** (`modules`, or `infrastructure` for prisma), and **skipping** the ❌ cells. For `ledger`, decide yourself whether it gets a controller. That's question G1.

**Order matters slightly:** always generate the **module first**. The service and controller generators look for that module and register themselves in it automatically.

When you're done, paste the `imports` array from `app.module.ts` and the startup logs, along with your answers to G1 and G2.

Before the Prisma module, there are some problems in what's been generated so far. Let's fix those first, because the build is currently broken.

## 🔍 Review of the current state

I read `src/` and `app.module.ts`:

| Problem | What happened |
|---|---|
| ❌ **The build is broken** | `app.module.ts` imports `./modules/customer/customer.controller.js` (singular **customer**), but that folder doesn't exist. I'm guessing you generated it, then deleted it and regenerated as `customers`. The import stayed behind. |
| ❌ **`CustomersModule` and `TransfersModule` are empty** (`@Module({})`) | Their services and controllers were generated **before** their modules existed, so the CLI registered them in **`AppModule`** instead. |
| ❌ **`accounts` has only a controller** | No `accounts.module.ts` or `accounts.service.ts`, and `AccountsController` is registered in `AppModule`. |
| 🟡 `notification` vs `notifications` | The design doc says `notifications`. Pick one name and stay consistent. |
| ✅ `auth`, `kyc`, `ledger` | Wired correctly. Ledger has no controller, so that's your G1 decision. We'll discuss it. |

That's the **"generate the module first"** rule from my last message, seen in practice. 🙂 It's a good thing to learn by hitting it.

### Fix it by hand (good practice for understanding module wiring)
1. **Delete the dead import** of `CustomerController` (singular) from `app.module.ts`.
2. **Accounts:** generate the missing module and service. The controller file already exists.
3. **Move registrations to their own modules.** In `customers.module.ts` and `transfers.module.ts`, add their `providers: [...]` and `controllers: [...]` with the matching imports, the same way `auth.module.ts` does it. Then do the same for `AccountsController` in the new `accounts.module.ts`.
4. **Clean up `AppModule`.** Its `controllers` should be just `[AppController]` and its `providers` just `[AppService]`. Its `imports` lists the **modules**. `AppModule` should only *assemble* modules, never own their parts.

### ⚠️ One more: `ObserveModule` with credentials in the code
The Nest 12 scaffold added `@nestjs/observe`, a **paid third-party telemetry service**, with `appKey`/`appSecret` placeholders **written directly in source code**. Two problems:
- **Secrets never go in code.** They belong in environment variables. If you ever filled those in and pushed, they'd be public.
- You'd be sending telemetry to an external service you haven't chosen.

**My recommendation:** remove the `ObserveModule` lines and the `@nestjs/observe` package for now. We'll build observability properly with **OpenTelemetry** in Phase 8, a vendor-neutral standard that's a stronger skill for your CV.

---

# Now: the Prisma module

## The concept
Every module that touches the database needs **one shared database client** with a lifecycle: connect at startup, disconnect at shutdown. NestJS does this with a **`PrismaService`** that *is* a `PrismaClient`, wrapped in a `PrismaModule` that other modules import.

There are three Prisma 7 specifics you need to know:
1. Prisma 7 talks to Postgres through a **driver adapter**, `@prisma/adapter-pg`, which uses the standard `pg` driver.
2. The client is **generated code**. You run `prisma generate`, and it writes TypeScript into the `output` folder from your `schema.prisma`.
3. NestJS **doesn't read `.env` on its own.** You need `@nestjs/config`.

## Step A: install (same version discipline as before)
```bash
npm i @prisma/adapter-pg@7.10.1 --save-exact
```
```bash
npm i @nestjs/config --save-exact
```

## Step B: move the generated client inside `src/`
Your `schema.prisma` currently has `output = "../generated/prisma"`, which is **outside** `src/`. Your `tsconfig.build.json` only compiles `src/`, so imports from there will fail at build time.

1. Change the output to `"../src/generated/prisma"`.
2. In `.gitignore`, replace `/generated/prisma` with `/src/generated/`. Generated code is never committed, because it's rebuilt from the schema.
3. Generate it:
   ```bash
   npx prisma generate
   ```

## Step C: generate the module and service
```bash
npx nest g module prisma infrastructure
```
```bash
npx nest g service prisma infrastructure
```

## Step D: write `PrismaService`
This is version-specific plumbing, so here it is. **Type it yourself** rather than pasting, and read the comments as you go:

```ts
// src/infrastructure/prisma/prisma.service.ts
import { Injectable, OnModuleDestroy, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { PrismaPg } from '@prisma/adapter-pg';
import { PrismaClient } from '../../generated/prisma/client.js';

@Injectable()
export class PrismaService
  extends PrismaClient // PrismaService IS the client: this.prisma.account.findMany() etc.
  implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy
{
  constructor(config: ConfigService) {
    super({
      // Prisma 7: queries go through the pg driver adapter
      adapter: new PrismaPg({
        connectionString: config.getOrThrow<string>('DATABASE_URL'), // fail fast if missing
      }),
    });
  }

  async onModuleInit() {
    await this.$connect(); // fail at startup, not on the first customer request
  }

  async onModuleDestroy() {
    await this.$disconnect(); // release connections on shutdown
  }
}
```

## Step E: wire it up
- **`prisma.module.ts`:** add `exports: [PrismaService]`. This is the answer to half of **G2**. Without `exports`, no other module can inject it.
- **`app.module.ts`:** add `ConfigModule.forRoot({ isGlobal: true })` to `imports`, so `.env` is loaded once for the whole app.

## Step F: verify
```bash
npm run build
```
```bash
npm run start:dev
```
You should see `PrismaModule dependencies initialized`, with no errors. As a test, temporarily rename `DATABASE_URL` in `.env`. The app should **refuse to start** with a clear error. That's `getOrThrow` doing its job. Then rename it back.

---

## 🧠 Design question
> **P1. Global or explicit?** NestJS lets you mark `PrismaModule` as `@Global()`, so every module can inject `PrismaService` without importing `PrismaModule`. That's convenient. Should you? Think about the rule *"only the owner writes to its tables"*, and about how you'd notice, from a module's `imports` list, which modules touch the database.

Paste your build and startup output when you're done, plus answers to **G1, G2 and P1**.

content.text:
Four errors, but really only **two causes**. Learning to spot **cascading errors** is the skill here.

## Read them as cause → effect

| # | Error | Cause |
|:---:|---|---|
| 1 | `Cannot find name 'ConfigModule'` | 🔴 **Cause A:** you used `ConfigModule` in `app.module.ts` but never **imported** it at the top of the file |
| 2 | `Cannot find module '../../generated/prisma/client.js'` | 🔴 **Cause B:** the client was never generated where the import expects it |
| 3 | `Property '$connect' does not exist` | ⚪ **Effect of #2.** TypeScript can't find `PrismaClient`, so it doesn't know what `PrismaService` extends, so it doesn't know about `$connect` |
| 4 | `Property '$disconnect' does not exist` | ⚪ **Same effect of #2** |

> 🎓 **Debugging habit:** compiler errors often **cascade**. Fix the **first root cause** and rebuild. Half the remaining errors usually disappear by themselves. Don't try to fix #3 and #4 directly; they aren't real problems.

## Fix A: the missing import
Every name you use in a TypeScript file has to be imported. `ConfigModule` comes from the package you just installed, `@nestjs/config`. Add the import line at the top of `app.module.ts`, next to the other imports.

## Fix B: Step B was skipped
I checked:
- `schema.prisma` still says `output = "../generated/prisma"`.
- So the client was generated into **`/generated/prisma` at the project root**, and `src/generated/` doesn't exist.
- `PrismaService` is looking in `src/generated/prisma`.

**Do Step B from my last message:**
1. Change the `output` in `prisma/schema.prisma` to `"../src/generated/prisma"`. The path is relative to the `prisma/` folder, so `..` goes up one level to the root, then into `src/`.

content.text:
Clean build. ✅ **Zero errors.** Both root causes are fixed, and the cascade errors (#3 and #4) disappeared by themselves, as expected.

Now for the wiring fix, explained properly.

---

## The idea: modules are departments

Think of the app as a **company**:
- **`AppModule`** is the **head office**. It only decides *which departments exist*.
- **Each module** (Accounts, Customers, …) is a **department**. It owns its staff: **controllers** (the front desk, handling HTTP requests) and **providers/services** (the back office, doing the work).

Right now your head office has **hired the staff of four departments directly**, while those departments sit there **empty**:

```
AppModule (head office)
├── imports:     AccountsModule ──► @Module({})   ← empty department
│                CustomersModule ─► @Module({})   ← empty department
│                TransfersModule ─► @Module({})   ← empty department
│                NotificationsModule ► @Module({}) ← empty department
├── controllers: AccountsController, CustomersController, TransfersController   ← wrong place
└── providers:   CustomersService, TransfersService, AccountsService, NotificationsService  ← wrong place
```

(This happened because each service and controller was generated **before** its module existed, so the CLI fell back to `AppModule`.)

## Why it matters, even though it builds

| Problem | What goes wrong |
|---|---|
| **Fake boundaries** | `AccountsModule` *claims* to be the Accounts department but contains nothing. Module boundaries (design doc section 7) only exist if the code lives inside them. |
| **Dependency injection breaks later** | When `AccountsService` needs `PrismaService`, NestJS looks in **the module that registers `AccountsService`**, which is currently `AppModule`. So you'd add `PrismaModule` there, and *everything* gets database access. Your boundary rules stop meaning anything. |
| **Duplicate instances** 🐛 | If you later *also* register `AccountsService` inside `AccountsModule`, NestJS creates **two separate instances**, one per module. Any state or caching splits silently. |
| **Phase 7 gets harder** | Extracting a microservice means lifting a module out whole. If its parts are scattered in `AppModule`, there's nothing clean to lift. |

---

## The target: what each file should look like

`auth.module.ts` and `kyc.module.ts` are **already correct**, so use them as your reference. Every department should look like this:

### `accounts.module.ts` (example)
```ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AccountsService } from './accounts.service.js';
import { AccountsController } from './accounts.controller.js';

@Module({
  controllers: [AccountsController], // front desk: HTTP routes
  providers: [AccountsService],      // back office: business logic
})
export class AccountsModule {}
```

**Now you do the same for:**

| File | `controllers` | `providers` |
|---|---|---|
| `customers.module.ts` | `CustomersController` | `CustomersService` |
| `transfers.module.ts` | `TransfersController` | `TransfersService` |
| `notifications.module.ts` | *(none)* | `NotificationsService` |

Don't forget the matching `import … from './….js'` lines at the top of each file. The `.js` extension is required, even though the files are `.ts`, because your project uses Node's ESM module resolution (`"type": "module"`, `nodenext`).

### `app.module.ts`: the head office only lists departments
When you're done, it should contain only this:
- **imports:** `ConfigModule.forRoot(...)`, `PrismaModule`, and the 8 domain modules
- **controllers:** `[AppController]` only
- **providers:** `[AppService]` only

Then **delete the import lines** at the top for everything you removed: `AccountsController`, `CustomersService`, `CustomersController`, `TransfersController`, `TransfersService`, `AccountsService`, `NotificationsService`. An import of something you no longer use is dead code, and your linter will flag it.

### Removing `ObserveModule`
In `app.module.ts`:
1. Delete `import { createObserveModule } from '@nestjs/observe';`
2. Delete the line `export const { ObserveModule, ObserveInstrument } = createObserveModule();`

Then remove the package itself:
```bash
npm uninstall @nestjs/observe
```

---

## How to check it's right
1. ```bash
   npm run build
   ```
2. ```bash
   npm run start:dev
   ```
3. In the startup logs, check two things:
   - `[InstanceLoader] AccountsModule dependencies initialized`, with one line per module.
   - `[RoutesResolver] AccountsController {/accounts}`. Each controller should be mapped, and **none twice**.
4. Commit with something like `refactor: move providers and controllers into their own modules`.

> 🎓 **Rule to remember:** `AppModule` **composes** modules and never **owns** their parts. If you see a domain service or controller in `AppModule`'s `providers` or `controllers`, something is wired wrong.

Paste the startup logs when you're done, along with **G1, G2 and P1** whenever you're ready.

content.text:
## Review: 2 correct, 1 to challenge

### ✅ G1: AccountsController, correct
The route belongs to the **customer's view** ("my account's history"), so `AccountsController` serves it. The **data** belongs to the Ledger, so `AccountsService` *asks* `LedgerService` for it (`getBalance`, `getHistory`).

The rule applies to **reads too**. If Accounts queried ledger tables directly, it would break as soon as the Ledger changed its schema, and in Phase 7 the Ledger becomes a separate service whose tables nobody else can reach.

**Only the owner touches its tables, for reads *and* writes.** Option 3 ("reading is harmless") was the trap.

### ✅ G2: export only LedgerService, correct
`exports: [LedgerService]` makes its **public methods the only way in**. Exporting `PrismaService` alongside it would hand everyone direct table access and undo the boundary. Leaving exports **empty** wouldn't work at all: NestJS would throw `Nest can't resolve dependencies of TransfersService` at startup.

Both are recorded ✅ in [DESIGN.md](docs/DESIGN.md), section 7.

### 🟡 P1: `@Global()`, valid but debatable, so let me challenge it
This one isn't simply right or wrong. **Many real NestJS codebases do make Prisma global**, so you can defend it. Here's the trade-off:

| | `@Global()` | Explicit imports |
|---|---|---|
| Boilerplate | Less: no `imports: [PrismaModule]` per module | A bit more |
| Visibility | ❌ You **can't see** which modules touch the database, because any module can inject it silently | ✅ A module's `imports` **tells you** it has database access |
| Enforcing boundaries | ❌ Nothing stops `TransfersService` from injecting `PrismaService` and writing `ledger_lines` itself | ✅ Code review catches it: *"why does Transfers import PrismaModule and write ledger tables?"* |
| NestJS guidance | The docs say global modules should be used **sparingly**, for truly app-wide plumbing (config, logging) | Matches the default |
| Phase 7 extraction | Harder to see each module's real dependencies | Dependencies are explicit, so lifting a module out is easier |

The key point for **this** project: you've built your whole design on **"only the owner writes."** `@Global()` makes the database available to **everyone** by default, which works against that rule. The explicit-import version doesn't *prevent* misuse either, but it makes it **visible**, and visibility is what code review relies on.

> One misconception to clear up, since it was an option: **"Only in AppModule" doesn't work.** NestJS modules **don't inherit** imports from their parent. Each module only sees what **it** imports (or what's `@Global()`).

**My recommendation:** use **explicit imports** for this project. It's a deliberate choice that matches your design doc.

**Your call:** keep `@Global()` or switch to explicit imports? If you keep it, reply with **one sentence defending it** and I'll record it in the design doc with the trade-off. Being able to defend a decision matters more than which one you pick.

---

## Before the next step
Still to fix from my last message:
1. **`TransfersModule`** is still empty. Register its controller and service.

4. Add **`exports: [LedgerService]`** to `ledger.module.ts`, following your G2 answer.

Then commit. Once that's in, we start designing the **Prisma schema** together. That's where your money rules, ledger model and NUBAN decisions become real tables. 🏦

|---|---|
| `TransfersModule` wired | ✅ Controller and service registered |

## ❌ 1. One failing test
```
FAIL  src/infrastructure/prisma/prisma.service.spec.ts
Nest can't resolve dependencies of the PrismaService (?).
Please make sure that the argument ConfigService at index [0] is available in the RootTestModule
```

**What this means:** the CLI generated this test *before* you added `ConfigService` to the constructor. The test builds a tiny NestJS module containing only `PrismaService`. When NestJS tries to create it, it asks *"who gives me a `ConfigService`?"*, and nobody in that test module does.

**This is the C1 benefit you named, in practice:** dependency injection lets you **swap real dependencies for fakes** in tests. You don't want a unit test that depends on your real `.env`, so give the test a **fake `ConfigService`**.

**Your task:** in `prisma.service.spec.ts`, find the `providers: [PrismaService]` line in `Test.createTestingModule(...)` and add a second provider. It should say *"when someone asks for `ConfigService`, use this object instead,"* where the object has a `getOrThrow` method returning a fake connection string. The NestJS pattern looks like this:

```ts
{ provide: ConfigService, useValue: { /* a fake getOrThrow here */ } }
```

You'll also need to import `ConfigService` at the top. Then run:
```bash
npm test
```
Expected result: **14 passed**.

> 💡 Why doesn't the test try to connect to the database? `compile()` creates the providers but **doesn't** run lifecycle hooks like `onModuleInit`, so `$connect()` is never called. A **unit** test shouldn't need a database. Tests that use a real database are **integration** tests, which come later.

## ❌ 2. `skills-lock.json` is ignored but still tracked
You added it to `.gitignore` 👍, but **`.gitignore` only affects files git isn't tracking yet.** This file was committed in your first commit, so git keeps tracking it. Tell git to stop tracking it while keeping it on disk:

```bash
git rm --cached skills-lock.json
```

> 🎓 This catches out a lot of developers. It's also why you **never** rely on `.gitignore` *after* committing a secret. Once it's in history, it's out. (That's part of the answer to **A3** from earlier.)

## 🟡 3. Uncommitted work and one open decision
- `ledger.module.ts` (the export) and `docs/DESIGN.md` (my updates) aren't committed yet.
- **P1 is still open:** keep `@Global()` with a one-sentence defence, or switch to explicit imports? Right now `PrismaModule` is **neither**: it isn't `@Global()`, and no module imports it yet. It doesn't matter until a service needs the database, which happens in the next step. So decide now.

## Then commit

```bash

content.text:
I fixed it, and all **14 of 14 tests pass** ✅. Lint is still clean.

## What I changed
In [prisma.service.spec.ts](src/infrastructure/prisma/prisma.service.spec.ts), I added a fake `ConfigService` to the test module:

```ts
providers: [
  PrismaService,
  {
    // Fake ConfigService so the unit test never reads the real .env
    provide: ConfigService,
    useValue: {
      getOrThrow: () => 'postgresql://test:test@localhost:5432/test',
    },
  },
],
```

I also added `import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';` at the top.

## How it works, line by line

| Piece | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `provide: ConfigService` | The **token**. It means: *"when anyone asks for a `ConfigService`…"* |
| `useValue: { … }` | *"…give them **this plain object** instead of the real class."* |
| `getOrThrow: () => '…'` | The fake only needs the **one method** `PrismaService` actually calls. NestJS doesn't check that it's a "real" `ConfigService`; it just has to work like one where it's used. |
| The fake URL | Never actually used for a connection. `compile()` doesn't run `onModuleInit`, so `$connect()` never fires. It only has to be a **valid-looking** string so `new PrismaPg(...)` doesn't complain. |

This is the **`useValue` provider pattern**, one of the most common testing techniques in NestJS. NestJS also has `useClass` (swap in a different class) and `useFactory` (build the value with a function). You'll use `useValue` constantly, for fake `LedgerService`s, fake `NotificationSender`s and so on.

> 🎓 **Why this matters for your C1 answer:** without dependency injection, `PrismaService` would read `.env` itself, and every test would need a real config file. With DI, **the test decides what the service receives.** That's the testability benefit you'd explain in an interview.

## Still left for you
1. **Untrack `skills-lock.json`:**
   ```bash
   git rm --cached skills-lock.json
   ```
2. **Decide P1:** keep `@Global()` (with a one-sentence defence) or use explicit imports.
3. **Commit everything:**
   ```bash
   git status
   ```
   You should see the spec, `ledger.module.ts` and `DESIGN.md` modified, and `skills-lock.json` deleted. Then:
   ```bash
   git add .
   ```
   ```bash
   git commit -m "fix: export LedgerService, mock ConfigService in Prisma spec, untrack skills-lock"
   ```

Then we move on to **designing the Prisma schema**. 🏦

questions.question: S1, what type should primary keys (IDs) be for customers, accounts, transfers and so on?

options.label: Auto-increment int
options.description: 1, 2, 3… Small, fast and simple. Exposed in URLs like /accounts/42.

options.label: UUID v4
options.description: Random 128-bit IDs like 9f1c… Unguessable, and can be generated anywhere.

options.label: UUID v7
options.description: 128-bit IDs that are time-ordered: unguessable like UUIDs, but they sort by creation time, which keeps database indexes efficient.

options.label: NUBAN as the key
options.description: Use the 10-digit account number itself as the accounts table's primary key.

questions.question: S2, how should the ledger be structured in tables?

options.label: One transactions table
options.description: Each row: from_account, to_account, amount, fee. Simple, one row per transfer.

options.label: Journal + lines
options.description: journal_entries (one row per event: id, type, reference, created_at) + ledger_lines (2+ rows each: account, debit/credit, amount). Every entry's lines must balance.

options.label: Entries with balance
options.description: One entries table where each row stores account, signed amount and the running balance after it.

questions.question: S3, ledger rows are written once. How should the database protect them?

options.label: App code only
options.description: Services simply never call update or delete on ledger tables; we trust the code.

options.label: Append-only in DB
options.description: Also enforce it in Postgres: a trigger (or restricted DB role) rejects any UPDATE or DELETE on ledger tables. Corrections are new reversal entries.

options.label: Soft delete
options.description: Add a deleted_at column so rows can be hidden without being removed.

options.label: Updatable + audit log
options.description: Allow updates, but copy the old values into an audit table first.

### Decisions

| # | Decision | Status |

| Rejected | Problem |
|---|---|
| Auto-increment IDs | `/accounts/42` invites guessing other IDs (IDOR attacks) and leaks business volume |
| UUID v4 | Random order scatters inserts across the index, so writes slow down at scale |

Not every ledger account belongs to a customer, e.g. **Fee income** and **Settlement**. So the Ledger keeps its own `ledger_accounts` table:

| Column | Notes |
|---|---|
| `id` | UUID v7 |
| `account_id` | Links to `accounts.id` for customer accounts; `NULL` for internal accounts |
| `code` | e.g. `FEE_INCOME`, `SETTLEMENT_NGN`, for internal accounts |
| `type` | `ASSET` · `LIABILITY` · `REVENUE` · `EXPENSE` · `EQUITY` |
| `currency` | ISO-4217, e.g. `NGN` |
| `balance` | `BIGINT` minor units: the cached balance, updated in the same transaction as the lines |

### Entity overview

```mermaid
erDiagram

    customers ||--o| credentials : "logs in with"
    customers ||--o{ kyc_verifications : submits

    journal_entries ||--|{ ledger_lines : "has 2+"
    ledger_accounts ||--o{ ledger_lines : "posted to"
    transfers ||--|| journal_entries : "recorded as"
```

### Ledger line rules

- `amount` is a **positive** `BIGINT` (`CHECK (amount > 0)`) with a separate `direction`: `DEBIT` or `CREDIT`
- Each line carries a `currency`, and every line in one entry uses the **same** currency
- **Σ debits = Σ credits** per journal entry, checked in `LedgerService` before commit

content.text:
Good choices on all four. **P1 is decided: explicit imports** ✅. That's the one I'd have recommended, because it keeps database access **visible**.

You asked me to recommend the other three, so here are the industry-standard choices and the reasons behind each. I've recorded all of them in a new **section 8, Data Model**, in [DESIGN.md](docs/DESIGN.md).

## S1: Primary keys → **UUID v7**, with NUBAN as a separate business key

There are two "standards" in play, and a well-built system uses **both**, for different jobs:

| Identifier | Standard | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **`id`** (primary key) | **UUID v7** (RFC 9562, a global standard since 2024) | Internal references, foreign keys, API URLs |
| **`account_number`** | **NUBAN** (the CBN's Nigerian standard) | What customers see, type and share. `UNIQUE`, but **never** the primary key |

**Why UUID v7?**
- **Unguessable.** `/accounts/42` invites attackers to try `/accounts/43`. That attack is called **IDOR** (insecure direct object reference), and it's a classic fintech vulnerability.
- **Time-ordered.** New IDs sort after old ones, so Postgres indexes stay compact. Random UUID v4s scatter inserts all over the index and slow writes down at scale.
- **Can be generated anywhere,** in the app, without asking the database. That's useful for idempotency and events later.

**Why not NUBAN as the primary key?** Primary keys must **never change**, and business identifiers sometimes do (migrations, re-numbering, errors).

## S2: Ledger structure → **journal + lines**
This is the standard **double-entry** shape used in banking ledgers and ledger products like Modern Treasury and Formance:
- **`journal_entries`**: one row per financial **event** ("Transfer #123", "Fee", "Reversal of #123").
- **`ledger_lines`**: two or more rows per entry. Each has a ledger account, a direction (debit or credit) and a positive amount, and **the lines must balance**.

Your Q3 example (A → B with a fee) is **one entry with three lines**. A single `transactions` table with from/to/amount can't represent that cleanly.

## S3: Immutability → **append-only, enforced in Postgres**
Application code saying "we never update ledger rows" isn't enough. One bug, one careless script, or one engineer in a SQL console can rewrite financial history. So we use **defence in depth**:
1. The app never calls update or delete on ledger tables.
2. **A Postgres trigger rejects any `UPDATE` or `DELETE`** on `journal_entries` and `ledger_lines`, so even a bug can't do it.
3. Mistakes are fixed with a **reversal entry**, never by editing.

## 🔄 One refinement to M1 (my correction)
Earlier we said the balance lives in `ledger_balances`, keyed by account ID. But your own Q3 answer has a **Fee Income** account, and that isn't a customer account. So the Ledger needs its own **chart of accounts**:

**`ledger_accounts`** holds *every* account money can sit in: customer accounts (linked to `accounts.id`) **and** internal accounts (`FEE_INCOME`, `SETTLEMENT_NGN`), each with a type (Asset, Liability, Revenue, …) and the cached `balance`.

I've updated the module table and the M1 decision to match. There's also an **entity diagram** in section 8.

---

## 🧠 Two checks before you write the schema

> **S4. Separating credentials.** Why should the **password hash** live in a separate `credentials` table owned by `AuthModule`, instead of a `password` column on `customers`? Think about who reads customer data, and what happens if that data leaks.
>
> **S5. Foreign keys across modules.** `accounts.customer_id` will be a foreign key to `customers.id`, but those tables have **different owners**. Is a database foreign key across module boundaries acceptable in the monolith? What happens to it in Phase 7, when Customers and Accounts become separate services with separate databases?

---

**`Customer`** (table `customers`)

| `id` | UUID v7 primary key |
| `email` | Optional, unique |
| `phone` | Optional, unique, in E.164 format (`+2348012345678`) |
| `firstName`, `lastName` | Required |
| `status` | Enum: `PENDING_VERIFICATION`, `ACTIVE`, `SUSPENDED`, `CLOSED`. Defaults to pending. |

**`Account`** (table `accounts`)

| `id` | UUID v7 primary key |
| `customerId` | Foreign key → `Customer` |
| `accountNumber` | Exactly 10 characters, unique (NUBAN) |

| `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `closedAt` (optional) | Timestamps |
| ⚠️ **no `balance`** | Remember M1 |

**Prisma syntax hints** (look these up in the Prisma docs):
- `@id @default(uuid(7)) @db.Uuid`: a UUID v7 primary key stored as Postgres's native `uuid` type
- `@unique`, `@db.Char(10)`, `@default(now())`, `@updatedAt`
- `@relation(fields: [...], references: [...])` for the foreign key
- `@@map("customers")` and `@map("first_name")`: TypeScript uses camelCase while Postgres tables and columns use snake_case. That's the industry convention.
- An `enum` block for each status and type

Good news first: I ran `npx prisma validate` on your current file and it **passes** 🚀. You'd already fixed that error by adding `accounts Account[]` to `Customer`.

**What the error was teaching:** Prisma relations are **two-sided**. `Account.customer` points to a `Customer`, so `Customer` must have the **opposite side**, a list of its accounts. The database only stores the `customer_id` column; the list field exists only in Prisma, so you can write queries like `customer.accounts`. `npx prisma format` adds it for you automatically.

Valid isn't the same as **correct**, though. Here's my review.

---

## 🔴 Critical: a money bug

```prisma
balance       Float       @default(0)
```

This one line breaks **two** of your own design decisions:
1. **Q1, money rules:** `Float` for money. That's the `0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004` problem.
2. **M1, balance ownership:** the balance lives in the **Ledger's** `ledger_accounts` table, not on `accounts`.

**Fix:** delete the line completely. `Account` should have **no balance at all**.

> 🎓 This is why the design doc exists. In a real code review I'd reject this pull request with *"violates DESIGN.md §2 and §7."* Re-read the relevant section of your design before writing each model.

## 🟠 Spec mismatches

| # | Issue | Your code | Should be |
|:---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Enum values | `inactive`, `suspended` (lowercase), and no `ACTIVE` | `PENDING_VERIFICATION`, `ACTIVE`, `SUSPENDED`, `CLOSED`. Keep all values **uppercase**, consistently. |
| 2 | Email and phone are required | `String @unique` | **Optional**: `String? @unique`. Customers sign up with email **or** phone. *(Postgres allows many `NULL`s in a unique column, so optional + unique works.)* |
| 3 | Account `status` missing | — | An `AccountStatus` enum (`ACTIVE`, `FROZEN`, `CLOSED`) and a `status` field with a default |

## 🟡 Database precision (these matter at scale)

| # | Issue | Why it matters | Fix |
|:---:|---|---|---|
| 4 | UUIDs stored as text | Without `@db.Uuid`, Postgres stores `id` as **text** (36 bytes) instead of native `uuid` (16 bytes), so indexes are bigger and comparisons slower | Add `@db.Uuid` to **every** UUID field, **including `customerId`**. Both sides of a foreign key must be the same type. |
| 5 | Unbounded strings | `accountNumber` and `currency` can hold any length | `@db.Char(10)` and `@db.Char(3)`. Let the database **reject** a 9-digit account number. |
| 6 | Naming | Tables become `Customer`/`Account` and columns `firstName` | Add `@@map("customers")` and `@@map("accounts")` to the models, and `@map("first_name")`, `@map("customer_id")` and so on to multi-word fields. Postgres convention is snake_case. |
| 7 | No index on `customerId` | ⚠️ **Postgres does NOT automatically index foreign keys.** "List this customer's accounts" would scan the whole table. | Add `@@index([customerId])` to `Account` |

### 🎓 Optional but good practice
- **Be explicit about deletes:** add `onDelete: Restrict` to the relation. Customers in a bank are **closed**, never deleted, so the database should refuse to delete a customer who still has accounts. Making it explicit shows the choice was deliberate.
- Remove the `npx create-db` comment at the top. That's Prisma's ad for its hosted database, not part of your schema.

---

## When you're done
```bash
npx prisma format
```
```bash
npx prisma validate
```
Then tell me to review it again.

Done. ✅ The schema **formats and validates** 🚀. I also kept the fixes you'd already made: no `balance`, uppercase enums, optional email and phone. 👏

## What I changed

| # | Fix | Before → after |
|:---:|---|---|
| 4 | **Native UUID type** | `@default(uuid(7))` → `@default(uuid(7)) @db.Uuid` on both `id`s **and** on `customerId` |
| 4 | **Fixed an invalid default** | `Customer.id` had `@default(db.uuid(7))`. That mixes up two different things: `uuid(7)` is the **default value**, and `@db.Uuid` is the **column type**. They're separate attributes. |
| 5 | **Fixed lengths** | `accountNumber` → `@db.Char(10)`, `currency` → `@db.Char(3)` |
| 6 | **snake_case in Postgres** | `@@map("customers")`, `@@map("accounts")`, plus `@map("first_name")`, `@map("customer_id")`, `@map("account_number")`, `@map("created_at")` and so on |
| 7 | **Foreign key index** | `@@index([customerId])` on `Account` |

### What `@map` gives you
Your TypeScript code still says `customer.firstName` and `account.customerId`. Prisma translates to `first_name` and `customer_id` in SQL. So **both worlds follow their own conventions**:
- When you write **raw SQL** for the row lock (`SELECT … FOR UPDATE`), you'll write `ledger_accounts`, `customer_id` and so on.
- DBAs, analytics tools and other languages reading the database see normal Postgres naming.

### Why `@db.Char(10)` matters
Without it, `accountNumber` is a Postgres `text` column, and a buggy generator could save `"12345"` or `"123456789012"`. With `CHAR(10)`, the **database itself** enforces the length. That's the same **defence in depth** idea as S3. Your app validates it, and the database is the last line.

> ⚠️ `CHAR(10)` checks **length**, not **content**. `"ABCDEFGHIJ"` would still pass. Making sure it's only digits with a valid NUBAN check digit is the app's job. A `CHECK (account_number ~ '^[0-9]{10}$')` constraint in the migration SQL would add a database-level backstop. We'll do that when we write the migration.

---

## 🟠 Still yours to do
1. **Account `status`:** add the `AccountStatus` enum (`ACTIVE`, `FROZEN`, `CLOSED`) and a `status` field on `Account` with a default. It's still missing.
2. **Optional:** `onDelete: Restrict` on the relation.
3. **One more precision point I didn't apply, so you can try it:** Prisma's `DateTime` maps to `timestamp(3)` **without time zone** by default. For a bank, every timestamp should be **`@db.Timestamptz(3)`**. Why do you think that is? (Hint: servers, customers and regulators can be in different time zones, and clocks change.) Add it to every `DateTime` field.

Then:
```bash
npx prisma format
```
```bash
npx prisma validate
```

## 🧠 Still waiting
> **S4.** Why does the password hash belong in a separate `credentials` table (owned by `AuthModule`), not a `password` column on `customers`?
>
> **S5.** `accounts.customer_id` is a foreign key into a table owned by **another** module. Is that acceptable in the monolith? What happens to it in Phase 7?

If you'd like options to pick from for S4, S5 or the Timestamptz question, just say so.

questions.question: Timestamptz: why should a bank store every timestamp WITH time zone?

options.label: Saves storage
options.description: timestamptz uses less disk space than timestamp.

options.label: Unambiguous instant
options.description: It stores an exact moment in time (UTC internally), so '23:30' means the same instant on a Lagos server, a London server, and in a regulator's report, and daily limits / cut-offs aren't off by an hour.

options.label: Faster queries
options.description: Postgres indexes timestamptz faster than timestamp.

options.label: Required by Prisma
options.description: Prisma needs timestamptz to handle @updatedAt correctly.

questions.question: S4, why should the password hash live in a separate credentials table owned by AuthModule?

options.label: Smaller blast radius
options.description: Many modules and queries read customers (profiles, KYC, admin views, exports). Keeping the hash elsewhere means a leak or over-broad query on customers never exposes it, and only AuthModule can touch it.

options.label: Performance
